module_title: Advanced Analysis - Judicial Review of 9th Schedule and Anti-Defection
introduction: This advanced level provides an analytical study of the 9th Schedule (created to shield land reforms from courts) and the complex legal nuances of the 10th Schedule (Anti-defection), including landmark Supreme Court judgments.

core_concepts.title: Ninth Schedule & The First Amendment
core_concepts.description: Added by the '1st Amendment Act (1951)' to protect land reform and zamindari abolition laws from 'Judicial Review'. Initially, laws placed in this schedule could not be challenged on the grounds of violation of Fundamental Rights.

core_concepts.title: I.R. Coelho Case (2007)
core_concepts.description: A landmark Supreme Court judgment that destroyed the 'blanket immunity' of the 9th Schedule. The Court ruled that any law placed in the 9th Schedule AFTER April 24, 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati verdict) is open to judicial review if it violates the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.

core_concepts.title: Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection)
core_concepts.description: Added by the 52nd Amendment (1985). An MP/MLA is disqualified if they voluntarily give up party membership or vote against the party whip. The 91st Amendment (2003) added an exception: the law does not apply if at least 2/3rds of the party's members agree to a 'merger' with another party.

core_concepts.title: Kihoto Hollohan Case (1992)
core_concepts.description: The Supreme Court ruled that the decision of the Presiding Officer (Speaker/Chairman) regarding disqualification under the 10th Schedule is NOT final and is subject to judicial review. However, courts cannot intervene until the Speaker makes a final decision.

important_entities.name: Fourth Schedule (4th)
important_entities.significance: It allocates seats in the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) to various states and Union Territories (only Delhi, Puducherry, and J&K have representation) strictly based on their 'population'.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A nominated member (e.g., to the Rajya Sabha) can join any political party within '6 months' of taking their seat without being disqualified. However, if they join a party AFTER 6 months, they face immediate disqualification.
In Assertion-Reasoning questions, if a statement says 'Laws in the 9th Schedule cannot be challenged in court under any circumstances', mark it as FALSE. Post-2007, they absolutely can be challenged.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Knowing the exact years the new schedules were added helps in chronology-based questions.

exam_strategy_tips: UPSC frequently tests the historical context of the 9th Schedule (the friction between the Nehru government and the Judiciary regarding property rights).
Remember that the authority to decide disqualification under the 10th Schedule lies with the 'Presiding Officer' of the House, NOT the Election Commission or the President.
